text: Lesson one named failure modes as one of the four things that change at scale -- at real production volume, some component is statistically always degraded somewhere. This lesson covers the architectural response: designing for high availability, plus the failure modes an AI system adds on top of what any production software system already deals with.

A single region running at ninety-nine point nine percent uptime sounds solid, until you compute what that actually means: over five hundred twenty-five minutes of downtime a year -- almost nine hours, for a customer-facing assistant. Run two independent regions in an active-active configuration, where either one alone can serve all traffic, and the combined system only fails if both regions fail at the same time. The math changes completely: two regions, each individually no better than before, combine to under one minute of downtime a year.

But that result holds only as long as the two regions' failures are genuinely independent -- and that caveat is the entire catch, not a footnote. If both regions depend on the same upstream model API provider, the same shared authentication service, or the same cloud account's billing system, a failure in any of those shared dependencies takes both regions down at once, and the redundancy math silently stops being true. Real high-availability design spends as much effort finding and removing shared dependencies as it does standing up the second region.

An AI system serving requests through a third-party model API adds failure modes a database-backed application never has. A model API outage: the provider hosting the LLM goes down entirely, a dependency now sitting outside the company's own infrastructure. Rate limiting: even a fully healthy provider will fail requests once a negotiated limit is exceeded, often with no warning during a traffic spike. And silent quality degradation: the provider pushes a model update, the API keeps returning success, but answer quality quietly drops -- the hardest of the three to catch, because nothing looks broken.

The responses map directly to the problems. Multi-region handles an infrastructure-level outage the same way it would for any web application. Multi-provider is the AI-specific extension -- architecting the system so a second model provider can be substituted if the primary one has an outage, even if the outputs aren't perfectly identical. And graceful degradation is the honest fallback for when neither option is available: Northbeam's assistant could fall back to showing the matched support documents directly, with no LLM-generated summary -- a worse experience, but a functioning one, instead of a hard failure. Deciding what the degraded mode does, in advance, is real architectural work.
Next, we put this whole chapter together in one case study -- scaling a RAG assistant from one hundred users to one million.
